purpose: Developer-only baseline for non-destructive active-run compatibility. Not student results. Preserve answers and scores from existing learner state.

mc.prompt: A student recognizes a familiar voice. Which part of this description is perception?
options: Interpreting the sound as that person’s voice
mc.answer: Interpreting the sound as that person’s voice
mc.explanation: Perception assigns meaning to sensory information. Detection and transmission occur earlier.
mc.cue: Look for the step that gives the input meaning.

mc.prompt: Which pair correctly matches a receptor with its stimulus?
mc.answer: Mechanoreceptor — movement of inner-ear fluid
mc.explanation: Movement is a mechanical stimulus. Inner-ear hair cells are mechanoreceptors.
mc.cue: Match the form of energy, not the name of the organ.

writing.prompt: Use a different everyday example to distinguish sensory reception, sensation and perception. Name the receptor category.
writing.model: For a ringing bicycle bell, inner-ear mechanoreceptors respond to movement; I become aware of a sound; I interpret it as a bell warning me that a cyclist is approaching.

writing.prompt: Explain why not noticing a constant stimulus is not proof that the sensory system has stopped working.
writing.model: Adaptation and changes in attention can reduce awareness of a constant stimulus. Receptors and pathways may still be active, and a change in the stimulus can become noticeable.
criteria: New changes can still be detected

checks.title: Eye structures and the path of light

mc.prompt: Which route correctly follows light through the eye?
mc.answer: Cornea → pupil → lens → retina
mc.explanation: This is the main route with the humours omitted for brevity. Neural signals leave the retina through the optic nerve.
mc.cue: Start at the transparent front of the eye.

mc.prompt: A diagram labels the opening in the coloured ring as “iris.” What needs correcting?
options: The opening is the retina; the ring is the lens
The opening is the optic nerve
The opening is the pupil; the coloured ring is the iris
Both labels refer to the cornea
mc.answer: The opening is the pupil; the coloured ring is the iris
mc.explanation: Iris names the tissue that changes the size of the opening. Pupil names the opening.
mc.cue: Separate tissue from space.

writing.prompt: Trace a ray of light from outside the eye to the retina. Include both humours and explain the different roles of the iris and lens.
writing.model: Light passes through the cornea, aqueous humour, pupil, lens and vitreous humour to the retina. The iris controls pupil diameter and the amount of entering light. The lens adjusts the focus on the retina.

writing.prompt: Compare the sclera, choroid and retina. Give one function for each rather than only its location.
writing.model: The sclera protects and supports the eye; the choroid nourishes tissues and absorbs stray light; the retina contains photoreceptors and neurons that detect and process light information.

mc.prompt: A student looks from a distant tree to a nearby book. Which change supports the new focus?
options: Ciliary muscle relaxes; lens becomes flatter
Ciliary muscle contracts; lens becomes rounder
Optic nerve shortens to move the retina
mc.answer: Ciliary muscle contracts; lens becomes rounder
mc.explanation: Near accommodation reduces ligament tension and allows the lens to round.
mc.cue: Follow muscle action to ligament tension, then lens shape.

mc.prompt: Distant rays focus in front of the retina. Which correction matches this model?
options: Removing the iris to treat a cataract
mc.answer: A concave lens for myopia
mc.explanation: A concave lens diverges the rays before they enter the eye.
mc.cue: Does the correction need more or less initial convergence?

writing.prompt: Explain near accommodation as a four-step chain: muscle action, ligament tension, lens shape and optical effect.
writing.model: The ciliary muscle contracts, suspensory-ligament tension decreases, the lens becomes rounder, and its refractive power increases to focus a nearby object on the retina.

writing.prompt: Compare myopia and hyperopia using focal position and corrective lens type. Explain one correction rather than just naming it.
writing.model: Myopia focuses distant light in front of the retina and is corrected with a concave lens. Hyperopia focuses behind the retina without sufficient accommodation and is corrected with a convex lens. The concave lens spreads rays so they meet farther back.

mc.prompt: Which sequence follows the principal retinal information pathway?
mc.answer: Photoreceptor → bipolar cell → ganglion cell
mc.explanation: Information flows from photoreceptors through retinal circuits to ganglion cells.
mc.cue: Start with the cell that transduces light.

mc.prompt: Why is the optic disc a blind spot?
options: The lens focuses every image there
mc.answer: It lacks rods and cones
mc.explanation: No photoreceptors occupy the location where ganglion axons leave.
mc.cue: Ask which cells are missing at the nerve exit.

writing.prompt: Trace light and neural information through the simplified three-layer retina. Explain why their directions differ.
writing.model: Light enters from the vitreous side past ganglion and bipolar layers to rods and cones. After transduction, information travels through bipolar pathways to ganglion cells, whose axons form the optic nerve.

writing.prompt: Compare the fovea centralis with the blind spot. Include the receptors present or absent and the consequence for vision.
writing.model: The fovea has a dense cone population supporting sharp central vision. The optic disc has no rods or cones because fibres leave as the optic nerve, so light falling there is not detected.
criteria: Optic disc and absence of receptors

mc.prompt: Which structure immediately transfers ossicle movement into the inner-ear fluid?
mc.answer: Oval window
mc.explanation: The stapes moves at the oval window, creating pressure changes in cochlear fluid.
mc.cue: Follow the final ossicle.

mc.prompt: Where does hearing transduction occur?
options: At the outer surface of the sclera
In hair cells of the cochlear sensory apparatus
mc.answer: In hair cells of the cochlear sensory apparatus
mc.explanation: Hair-cell bending changes electrical activity and transmitter release to sensory neurons.
mc.cue: Look for the receptor rather than a conducting structure.

writing.prompt: Trace sound energy from the pinna to auditory-nerve activity. State where mechanical movement becomes a neural signal.
writing.model: Pinna → auditory canal → tympanum → malleus → incus → stapes → oval window → cochlear fluid and basilar-membrane movement → hair-cell bending → auditory sensory neurons. Hair cells transduce the movement and communicate with neurons that generate action potentials.

writing.prompt: Explain why the Eustachian tube is important even though it is not on the main route from the pinna to the organ of Corti.
writing.model: The tube links the middle ear to the throat region and helps equalize air pressure across the tympanum. That supports normal membrane vibration rather than directly carrying sound to the cochlea.

mc.prompt: The amplitude of a tone increases while its frequency stays constant. What should mainly change?
options: Pitch increases while loudness stays similar
Loudness increases while pitch stays similar
mc.answer: Loudness increases while pitch stays similar
mc.explanation: Amplitude and frequency are separate wave properties.
mc.cue: Which property counts cycles per second?

mc.prompt: High-frequency sounds most strongly stimulate which region in the source model?
options: The cochlear base near the oval window
mc.answer: The cochlear base near the oval window
mc.explanation: The high-frequency end is closest to the oval window.
mc.cue: Think of position along the basilar membrane.

writing.prompt: Explain why “high sound” is ambiguous. Use frequency, amplitude, pitch and loudness correctly in your answer.
writing.model: High may refer to frequency and perceived pitch, or to amplitude and perceived loudness. A loud low-frequency sound is possible, so the two properties must be described separately.

writing.prompt: A case states that hair cells are badly damaged but some auditory nerve fibres still work. Explain the principle behind an implant without promising a guaranteed outcome.
writing.model: An implant can bypass some damaged hair-cell function and stimulate remaining nerve fibres electrically. Useful perception depends on the remaining pathway and adaptation; it does not regrow hair cells or reproduce all natural hearing.

mc.prompt: Which structure is most directly associated with detecting a change in head rotation?
mc.answer: Semicircular canals
mc.explanation: Rotational changes deflect the canal cupula through relative fluid movement.
mc.cue: Separate rotation from straight-line movement.

mc.prompt: A lift begins moving upward. Which structure is particularly relevant?
mc.answer: Saccule
mc.explanation: The saccule contributes strongly to detection of vertical linear acceleration.
mc.cue: Identify the plane and type of movement.

writing.prompt: Compare the mechanism for a change in rotation with the mechanism for linear acceleration. Include the receptor, surrounding structure and source of movement.
writing.model: Rotation changes relative canal-fluid movement and deflects the cupula, bending hair cells. Linear acceleration shifts a weighted otolithic membrane in the utricle or saccule relative to hair cells. Both mechanisms alter sensory signalling.

writing.prompt: Explain why balance can become less reliable when visual information disagrees with vestibular information.
writing.model: The brain normally combines vision, vestibular signals and proprioception. Conflicting signals make its estimate of motion and position less consistent, which can disturb perceived balance.

mc.prompt: Why does food need to dissolve in saliva for taste detection?
options: Dissolved chemicals can interact with taste receptor cells
Saliva sends light to the fovea
Saliva converts every taste into sound
mc.answer: Dissolved chemicals can interact with taste receptor cells
mc.explanation: Taste is chemoreception: substances must reach receptor cells in a usable form.
mc.cue: Identify the kind of receptor.

mc.prompt: Which explanation best links dense touch representation to precise discrimination?
options: Larger action potentials always give finer detail
Small receptive fields and neural representation help separate nearby contacts
Every body region has identical receptor density
The back has no sensory receptors
mc.answer: Small receptive fields and neural representation help separate nearby contacts
mc.explanation: Touch precision depends on receptor distribution, receptive fields and processing.
mc.cue: Avoid explaining acuity only with impulse height.

writing.prompt: Explain how taste and smell both use chemoreception but start at different structures. Then connect them to flavour.
writing.model: Dissolved food chemicals stimulate taste receptor cells in taste buds. Odour molecules stimulate olfactory receptors and signals reach the olfactory bulb. The brain combines these inputs with texture and temperature to produce flavour perception.

writing.prompt: Plan, but do not perform, a fair touch-discrimination investigation. Include a question, prediction, changed variable, measured response, two controls and one safety requirement.
writing.model: Question: does touch discrimination differ by body region? Prediction: fingertips permit finer discrimination. Change region; measure correct discrimination using a teacher-approved method. Control contact pressure and instructions; repeat trials. Use only approved safe blunt materials under supervision, and do not invent results.

mc.prompt: A clear lens forms an image on a region of retina that lacks photoreceptors. What is the immediate limitation?
options: The pupil becomes a sensory neuron
There is no local photoreceptor transduction
mc.answer: There is no local photoreceptor transduction
mc.explanation: Focusing cannot replace receptors.
mc.cue: Identify the step after focusing.

mc.prompt: Which combination describes near accommodation?
options: Relaxed ciliary muscle, reduced tension, rounder lens
Relaxed ciliary muscle, increased tension, rounder lens
Contracted ciliary muscle, reduced ligament tension, rounder lens
Contracted ciliary muscle, increased tension, flatter lens
mc.answer: Contracted ciliary muscle, reduced ligament tension, rounder lens
mc.explanation: Ciliary contraction reduces the tension that flattens the lens.
mc.cue: Use the full four-step chain.

mc.prompt: Which pair correctly distinguishes hearing and rotation receptors?
options: Cochlear hair cells / semicircular-canal hair cells
mc.answer: Cochlear hair cells / semicircular-canal hair cells
mc.explanation: Both are mechanoreceptive systems but have different structures and stimuli.
mc.cue: Which apparatus responds to each kind of movement?

mc.prompt: A tone becomes higher in pitch without becoming louder. Which main wave property increases?
mc.answer: Frequency
mc.explanation: Frequency is the cycles-per-second property associated with pitch.
mc.cue: Separate pitch from loudness.

mc.prompt: Which route carries retinal information toward the brain?
options: Rods/cones → bipolar pathways → ganglion cells → optic nerve
mc.answer: Rods/cones → bipolar pathways → ganglion cells → optic nerve
mc.explanation: Ganglion-cell axons form the optic nerve.
mc.cue: Start with transduction, not with light entry.

mc.prompt: A study changes contact pressure and body region at the same time. Why is its conclusion limited?
options: Repeated trials would erase every confound
Either change could contribute to a difference in discrimination
Two variables always prove the same cause
mc.answer: Either change could contribute to a difference in discrimination
mc.explanation: A fair comparison controls other influential variables.
mc.cue: Ask whether the cause of the difference is isolated.

writing.prompt: Compare vision and hearing using four headings: original stimulus, conducting/focusing structures, receptor/transduction, and route to brain interpretation.
writing.model: Vision begins with light guided by cornea, humours, pupil and lens to retinal rods and cones; retinal processing leads to ganglion-cell activity and visual pathways. Hearing begins with pressure waves conducted by pinna, canal, tympanum and ossicles to cochlear movement; hair cells transduce movement and sensory neurons carry information into auditory pathways.
criteria: Neural transmission distinguished from original energy

writing.prompt: A student writes: “All balance comes from the semicircular canals, all tastes come from separate tongue regions, and the optic nerve carries light.” Correct each claim and explain the mechanism behind one correction.
writing.model: Balance combines semicircular canals, utricle/saccule, vision and proprioception. Taste categories are distributed, not confined to exclusive zones. The optic nerve carries ganglion-cell action potentials. For example, otolith organs use a weighted membrane to detect gravity and linear acceleration, rather than using the canal rotation mechanism.

mc.prompt: Which description best captures homeostasis?
options: Every internal variable stays exactly constant
The body stops responding to change
Only the nervous system controls internal conditions
Ongoing adjustments keep internal conditions within suitable ranges
mc.answer: Ongoing adjustments keep internal conditions within suitable ranges
mc.explanation: Homeostasis is dynamic regulation, not complete absence of variation.
mc.cue: Look for regulated ranges rather than a frozen value.

mc.prompt: What distinguishes the endocrine action of the pancreas from its exocrine action?
options: Hormones enter the blood rather than a digestive duct
Exocrine cells release all hormones into blood
Both actions send insulin to the small intestine
Only its endocrine cells make proteins
mc.answer: Hormones enter the blood rather than a digestive duct
mc.explanation: Endocrine and exocrine describe different routes of secretion.
mc.cue: Compare the delivery route.

writing.prompt: Compare nervous and endocrine communication using message type, delivery route and target specificity.
writing.model: Nervous communication uses electrical changes along neurons and chemical signals at junctions in defined pathways. Endocrine communication uses hormones in blood. Responsive target cells need appropriate receptors; wide hormone distribution does not mean a universal response.

writing.prompt: Choose an internal variable and explain why homeostasis does not mean that it never changes.
writing.model: Blood glucose can rise after a meal. Responses such as insulin secretion and glucose storage then bring it back toward a suitable range. Variation and active correction are part of homeostasis.

mc.prompt: A hormone cannot readily cross the lipid bilayer. What is the most likely signalling route?
options: Entering the nucleus without a receptor
Binding a membrane receptor that activates internal signalling
Becoming a steroid after binding blood
mc.answer: Binding a membrane receptor that activates internal signalling
mc.explanation: Cell-surface receptors allow external signals to change internal activity.
mc.cue: Match receptor location to membrane permeability.

mc.prompt: Which statement correctly describes cortisol?
options: It is a steroid hormone with intracellular receptor action
It is the receptor for insulin
mc.answer: It is a steroid hormone with intracellular receptor action
mc.explanation: Cortisol is produced from cholesterol and belongs to the steroid group.
mc.cue: Identify the chemical class.

writing.prompt: Compare water-soluble and steroid-hormone signalling. Include receptor location and how an internal response begins.
writing.model: Water-soluble hormones generally bind membrane receptors and trigger internal signalling. Steroid hormones can enter cells and bind intracellular receptors, influencing gene expression and protein production. Both require suitable target-cell machinery.

writing.prompt: A hormone is present at a normal concentration, but a target cell cannot respond. Give one mechanism that could explain this and distinguish it from hormone underproduction.
writing.model: A defective or absent receptor could prevent the cell from recognizing or signalling the hormone. This differs from a gland releasing too little hormone, where the receiving machinery may still work.

mc.prompt: Blood glucose falls, then glucagon-supported processes raise it. Which classification fits?
options: No regulation because a hormone is involved
Positive feedback because the response is useful
mc.answer: Negative feedback
mc.explanation: The return effect opposes the original fall.
mc.cue: Compare the response with the starting disturbance.

mc.prompt: Which feature distinguishes the labour example from ordinary negative feedback?
options: Contractions reinforce the stretch that supports further oxytocin release
Oxytocin is never released into blood
The response immediately eliminates the stimulus at every step
mc.answer: Contractions reinforce the stretch that supports further oxytocin release
mc.explanation: The loop reinforces itself until an endpoint changes the conditions.
mc.cue: Look for reinforcement, not simply a hormone increase.

writing.prompt: Explain negative feedback using a named variable that first falls. Identify the response and why it is negative feedback.
writing.model: If blood glucose falls, glucagon secretion rises and promotes glucose release from the liver. Blood glucose rises, opposing the original decrease and reducing the drive for the response.

writing.prompt: Explain the positive-feedback labour example and state what prevents it from continuing indefinitely.
writing.model: Cervical stretch promotes oxytocin release, which strengthens contractions and can increase stretch. Delivery changes or removes the stretch stimulus, interrupting the reinforcing loop.

mc.prompt: Which pairing correctly describes ADH?
options: Made in pancreatic beta cells; released from liver
Made in posterior pituitary; released from thyroid
Made in hypothalamus; released from posterior pituitary
Made in adrenal medulla; released from kidneys
mc.answer: Made in hypothalamus; released from posterior pituitary
mc.explanation: Production and release occur in different parts of the hypothalamic–posterior-pituitary pathway.
mc.cue: Pay attention to made versus released.

mc.prompt: Which hormone pair correctly distinguishes milk production from milk ejection?
mc.answer: Prolactin / oxytocin
mc.explanation: Prolactin supports synthesis of milk; oxytocin supports its ejection.
mc.cue: Do not treat production and release as synonyms.

writing.prompt: Compare the anterior and posterior pituitary using control route, hormone production and one example hormone from each.
writing.model: Hypothalamic regulatory hormones reach anterior-pituitary cells through portal blood; those cells make hormones such as TSH. ADH is made in hypothalamic neurons, transported along axons and released from the posterior pituitary.

writing.prompt: A student says oxytocin and prolactin are interchangeable because both relate to milk. Explain the error.
writing.model: Prolactin from the anterior pituitary supports milk production. Oxytocin made in the hypothalamus and released posteriorly supports milk ejection. The related target does not mean identical functions.

mc.prompt: Which condition makes gigantism possible in the standard hGH model?
mc.answer: Excess hGH before growth-plate closure
mc.explanation: Open growth plates permit excessive linear bone growth.
mc.cue: Focus on target-tissue status.

mc.prompt: Which relationship describes an indirect effect of hGH?
options: hGH stimulates liver growth-factor release that supports tissue growth
mc.answer: hGH stimulates liver growth-factor release that supports tissue growth
mc.explanation: Growth factors mediate important effects of hGH.
mc.cue: Identify an intermediate signal.

writing.prompt: Explain how excess hGH can produce gigantism in one case and acromegaly in another.
writing.model: Before growth plates close, excess hGH supports excessive linear bone growth and gigantism. After closure, bone and soft tissue enlarge without the same height increase, producing acromegaly.

writing.prompt: Describe a direct and an indirect part of the hGH pathway in general terms.
writing.model: hGH can alter metabolism directly in responsive tissues. It also stimulates liver growth-factor production, and these factors support growth in bone, cartilage and muscle.

mc.prompt: With normally responsive kidneys, increased ADH should produce…
options: Increased insulin synthesis in the kidney
More urine with a lower concentration
Less urine with a higher concentration
mc.answer: Less urine with a higher concentration
mc.explanation: Increased water reabsorption leaves less water in the urine.
mc.cue: Follow where water moves.

mc.prompt: What distinguishes nephrogenic from central diabetes insipidus in this lesson?
options: Both always mean absent posterior pituitary tissue
The retina makes ADH in nephrogenic cases
High glucose is required only in nephrogenic cases
Impaired kidney response rather than inadequate ADH availability
mc.answer: Impaired kidney response rather than inadequate ADH availability
mc.explanation: A missing hormone and a resistant target are different mechanisms.
mc.cue: Distinguish signal supply from target response.

writing.prompt: Trace the response to overly concentrated body fluids from detector to urine effect and feedback.
writing.model: Hypothalamic osmoreceptors detect increased concentration. More ADH is released from the posterior pituitary, increasing collecting-duct water permeability. More water is reabsorbed, urine volume falls and urine becomes more concentrated. Correction of body-fluid concentration reduces the stimulus.

writing.prompt: Explain why replacing a hormone could help a deficiency case but not fully solve a target-resistance case. Use ADH as the example.
writing.model: If ADH is deficient, replacing the signal can allow responsive kidneys to conserve water. If the kidneys are resistant, the signal may already be present but the target response is impaired, so replacement alone may not restore regulation.

mc.prompt: Primary thyroid failure occurs while pituitary control remains intact. Which pattern is expected?
options: Normal thyroid hormone in every case
High thyroid hormone and low TSH
Low thyroid hormone and no possible TSH rise
Low thyroid hormone and high TSH
mc.answer: Low thyroid hormone and high TSH
mc.explanation: Low output reduces feedback inhibition, allowing TSH to rise.
mc.cue: Use the word primary and the intact-pituitary condition.

mc.prompt: Why can inadequate iodine contribute to goitre?
options: The pancreas moves into the neck
Low thyroid output allows persistent TSH stimulation
Low TSH always makes the thyroid expand
Iodine directly becomes the whole pituitary
mc.answer: Low thyroid output allows persistent TSH stimulation
mc.explanation: Limited synthesis and reduced feedback can sustain gland stimulation.
mc.cue: Connect nutrient supply to the feedback loop.

writing.prompt: Trace the TRH–TSH–thyroid-hormone pathway and explain its negative feedback.
writing.model: TRH from the hypothalamus stimulates anterior-pituitary TSH, which stimulates thyroid-hormone secretion. Increased thyroid hormone inhibits upstream hypothalamic and pituitary stimulation. A fall reduces inhibition when the pathway is intact.

writing.prompt: Compare low thyroid hormone due to primary thyroid failure with low thyroid hormone due to pituitary failure. State the TSH distinction and your assumptions.
writing.model: With primary thyroid failure and intact pituitary response, TSH should rise because feedback is reduced. With pituitary failure, TSH may remain low or inappropriate for the low thyroid hormone. The same low final hormone can therefore have different causes.

mc.prompt: Low blood calcium most directly stimulates which response?
options: Increased TSH as the only controller
Increased insulin as the main calcium hormone
mc.answer: Increased PTH release
mc.explanation: Parathyroid hormone acts to raise low blood calcium.
mc.cue: Name the gland that senses this variable.

mc.prompt: How does PTH indirectly increase intestinal calcium absorption?
options: By promoting activation of vitamin D
mc.answer: By promoting activation of vitamin D
mc.explanation: Active vitamin D supports absorption from the intestine.
mc.cue: Look for an intermediate signal.

writing.prompt: Trace the response to low blood calcium. Include PTH’s source and effects involving bone, kidney and intestine.
writing.model: Parathyroid glands release PTH. It promotes mobilization of calcium from bone, increases kidney calcium reabsorption and supports vitamin D activation, indirectly increasing intestinal absorption. Rising blood calcium reduces the stimulus for release.

writing.prompt: Explain how PTH and calcitonin are antagonistic without describing them as identical systems with reversed arrows.
writing.model: PTH raises blood calcium, while calcitonin can lower it. Their overall effects oppose one another, but PTH is more important in adult human regulation and their detailed targets and control are not perfect mirror images.

mc.prompt: Which route correctly describes rapid adrenal hormone release?
mc.answer: Sympathetic neurons → adrenal medulla → epinephrine
mc.explanation: The medulla is directly stimulated by sympathetic input.
mc.cue: Look for the neural-to-endocrine connection.

mc.prompt: Why does liver glycogen breakdown support an acute stress response?
options: It lowers every tissue’s energy needs to zero
It makes glucose available to the blood
mc.answer: It makes glucose available to the blood
mc.explanation: Glucose availability helps meet increased fuel demands.
mc.cue: Connect the storage form to the available fuel.

writing.prompt: Trace the rapid adrenal stress pathway and explain two effects in terms of immediate action.
writing.model: Sympathetic neurons stimulate the adrenal medulla, which releases epinephrine and norepinephrine. Increased cardiac activity supports transport; liver glycogen breakdown increases circulating glucose for fuel.

writing.prompt: Compare the adrenal medulla with the adrenal cortex without yet listing every cortical hormone.
writing.model: The medulla is the inner region and responds directly to sympathetic neural input, releasing catecholamine hormones. The cortex is outer glandular tissue producing steroid hormones through other control pathways.

mc.prompt: Which sequence correctly follows cortisol regulation?
options: Hypothalamic CRH → pituitary ACTH → adrenal-cortex cortisol
mc.answer: Hypothalamic CRH → pituitary ACTH → adrenal-cortex cortisol
mc.explanation: Each hormone has a defined source and target in the cortisol axis.
mc.cue: Locate the anterior-pituitary step.

mc.prompt: If cortisol rises in an intact feedback pathway, what tends to happen upstream?
mc.answer: CRH and ACTH stimulation decrease
mc.explanation: Cortisol restrains its upstream controllers by negative feedback.
mc.cue: Follow the inhibitory return arrows.

writing.prompt: Compare the rapid adrenal-medulla pathway with the cortisol pathway. Include the signal route and final hormones.
writing.model: The medulla receives direct sympathetic neural input and releases epinephrine/norepinephrine. The cortisol pathway uses hypothalamic CRH, anterior-pituitary ACTH and adrenal-cortex cortisol, with cortisol feeding back on upstream control.

writing.prompt: Explain how cortisol can support glucose availability and how feedback limits its own release.
writing.model: Cortisol supports metabolic processes that make fuel substrates available and promote liver glucose production. Increasing cortisol reduces CRH and ACTH stimulation in an intact pathway, restraining further release.
criteria: Metabolic action without direct fat-to-glucose shortcut

mc.prompt: What is aldosterone’s major direct kidney action in this course?
options: Make ADH in the collecting duct
Increase sodium reabsorption and potassium secretion
mc.answer: Increase sodium reabsorption and potassium secretion
mc.explanation: Aldosterone changes ion transport in distal kidney regions.
mc.cue: Identify the ion-handling mechanism.

mc.prompt: Which signals are emphasized in aldosterone’s main regulation?
options: Only insulin from the posterior pituitary
mc.answer: Angiotensin II and blood potassium
mc.explanation: Aldosterone does not simply share cortisol’s primary control pathway.
mc.cue: Separate two cortical hormones.

writing.prompt: Trace how aldosterone can support blood pressure. Include its source, kidney action and the connection between sodium and water.
writing.model: Aldosterone from the adrenal cortex increases kidney sodium reabsorption. Retaining sodium supports water retention and extracellular fluid volume, helping maintain blood volume and pressure.

writing.prompt: Compare ADH with aldosterone and explain why putting them both under “saves water” is incomplete.
writing.model: ADH is made in the hypothalamus and released posteriorly; it increases kidney water permeability. Aldosterone comes from the cortex and increases sodium reabsorption. Both can conserve volume, but sources, immediate targets and primary regulation differ.

mc.prompt: Which pairing correctly matches pancreatic cells to hormones?
options: Alpha cells — ADH; beta cells — cortisol
Beta cells — glucagon; alpha cells — insulin
Beta cells — insulin; alpha cells — glucagon
mc.answer: Beta cells — insulin; alpha cells — glucagon
mc.explanation: Cell identity and hormone role must stay linked.
mc.cue: Remember each cell’s regulated-glucose direction.

mc.prompt: Between meals, glucagon helps maintain blood glucose mainly by…
options: Blocking every form of liver glucose release
Turning the thyroid into a pancreas
Promoting liver glycogen breakdown and glucose production
Moving glucose into the lens as the main storage site
mc.answer: Promoting liver glycogen breakdown and glucose production
mc.explanation: The liver supplies glucose to circulation.
mc.cue: Distinguish glycogen, glucose and glucagon.

writing.prompt: Compare the response after a meal with the response between meals. Include alpha/beta cells, insulin/glucagon, liver action and feedback.
writing.model: After a meal, higher glucose stimulates beta-cell insulin, supporting uptake and storage and reducing glucose output. Between meals, falling glucose supports alpha-cell glucagon, promoting liver glycogen breakdown and glucose production. Each response opposes the initiating change.

writing.prompt: Compare diabetes mellitus with diabetes insipidus using their hormone mechanism rather than their shared symptoms.
writing.model: Diabetes mellitus involves inadequate insulin production/action and elevated glucose; glucose in the urine can increase water loss. Diabetes insipidus involves impaired water conservation, often from ADH deficiency or resistance, producing excessive dilute urine without requiring high glucose.
criteria: Shared symptoms do not imply same cause

checks.title: Integrated chapter review and final check

mc.prompt: Which production/release pair is correct?
mc.answer: ADH: hypothalamus / posterior pituitary
mc.explanation: Production and release are separate parts of the ADH pathway.
mc.cue: Read both verbs.

mc.prompt: Which observation best fits primary thyroid underproduction with intact control?
options: High T4 with low TSH proves pituitary failure
Low T4 always requires low TSH
mc.answer: Low T4 with elevated TSH
mc.explanation: Low thyroid output reduces feedback inhibition of TSH secretion.
mc.cue: Use the stated location of failure.

mc.prompt: Which response directly follows sympathetic stimulation of the adrenal medulla?
mc.answer: Epinephrine and norepinephrine release
mc.explanation: The medulla links sympathetic neural signals with catecholamine hormone release.
mc.cue: Separate medulla from cortex.

mc.prompt: A normally responsive kidney receives more ADH. Which urine change is expected?
options: No possible change in water handling
Higher glucose production in the lens
mc.answer: Lower volume and higher concentration
mc.explanation: More water is reabsorbed from the tubule.
mc.cue: Follow water back to blood.

mc.prompt: Which explanation of low blood calcium is appropriate?
options: Insulin is always the main correction
Calcitonin is the only response that raises calcium
The pituitary must convert glucose into calcium
Increased PTH helps conserve and mobilize calcium
mc.answer: Increased PTH helps conserve and mobilize calcium
mc.explanation: PTH supports bone mobilization, kidney conservation and indirect intestinal absorption.
mc.cue: Identify the controlled ion.

mc.prompt: Which statement about diabetes is most defensible?
options: Diabetes insipidus always requires high glucose
Type 2 means no insulin is ever present
Insulin deficiency and insulin resistance can both impair glucose regulation
mc.answer: Insulin deficiency and insulin resistance can both impair glucose regulation
mc.explanation: Mechanism is more informative than a rigid age or symptom rule.
mc.cue: Distinguish signal supply and response.

writing.prompt: Compare three responses: water loss, a carbohydrate-containing meal and an immediate threat. For each, name a relevant trigger, hormone source, target, effect and control relationship.
writing.model: Water loss/concentration change can increase posterior-pituitary ADH, changing kidney water permeability and conserving water. A meal can increase pancreatic beta-cell insulin, supporting tissue uptake and liver storage to lower glucose. Immediate threat can activate sympathetic neurons and adrenal-medulla catecholamines, supporting rapid fuel and cardiovascular responses.

writing.prompt: Correct this explanation: “ACTH controls every adrenal hormone; all hormones act on every cell; and low thyroxine always means high TSH.” Include the conditions that make your corrections necessary.
writing.model: ACTH chiefly supports cortisol secretion; aldosterone is mainly controlled by angiotensin II and potassium, while the medulla receives sympathetic input. Targets require suitable receptors. Low thyroxine produces high TSH in primary thyroid failure only when the pituitary can respond; upstream failure can produce a different pattern.
